errors.description: The model incorrectly inferred the trajectory order of the arrow. According to the Scene Description, the arrow moves from white → orange → yellow, not white → yellow → orange. This fundamental misordering of events led the model to analyze the wrong segment (white to yellow) as the first leg of the journey, when in fact it was the second leg (white to orange) that took the shortest time (0.50s). The model’s entire reasoning chain is built on this incorrect sequence.

errors.evidence_quote: Assuming the arrow moves at a constant speed (a standard assumption in such problems), shorter distance = shorter time.
errors.description: While assuming constant speed is reasonable in the absence of explicit timing data, the model applied this assumption to an incorrectly reconstructed trajectory. The premise is logically sound in isolation, but it was applied to a hallucinated spatial sequence (white→yellow→orange) rather than the actual observed sequence (white→orange→yellow). This compounds the error by using valid logic on invalid input.

analysis_result.analysis: The model failed primarily due to misordering the sequence of the arrow’s movement. It incorrectly assumed the arrow traveled from white to yellow first, when the Scene Description clearly states the arrow moved from white to orange (0:13–0:14, 0.50s), then orange to yellow (0:14–0:15, 1.00s). This error cascaded into selecting 'yellow' as the answer, when the correct answer is 'orange' — the shape reached in the shortest time from the previous shape. The model’s assumption of constant speed was reasonable but applied to an incorrect trajectory, rendering the conclusion invalid.
